content: Tormentil, scientifically known as Potentilla erecta, is a herbaceous perennial plant that belongs to the Rosaceae family, commonly referred to as the rose family. It is also known by the name septfoil. This plant is characterized by its low, clump-forming growth habit, with slender stems that can either trail along the ground or grow in an arching upright manner. The plant typically reaches a height of 10 to 30 cm and does not produce rooting runners. Tormentil is native to and grows wild across various regions of Asia and northern Europe. It thrives in a wide range of habitats, including clearings, meadows, sandy soils, and dunes. The flowering period of this plant extends from May to August or September. Its flowers are yellow, measuring 7 to 11 mm in diameter, and are borne singly at the tips of long stalks. Each flower usually has four notched petals, which is relatively uncommon within the rose family. These petals measure between 3 and 6 mm in length and are slightly longer than the sepals. The flowers also feature 20 to 25 stamens. The leaves of Tormentil are glossy and pinnately compound. The basal leaves, or radical leaves, are attached to the plant by long petioles, whereas the leaves on the stems are typically sessile or may have shorter petioles. Each leaf is composed of three obovate leaflets with serrated margins. The stipules of the plant are leaf-like and exhibit a palmate-lobed structure. The root system of Tormentil is rhizomatous and thick. The dried root of Tormentil has been historically used to prepare a medicinal lotion. This preparation has been employed to treat various conditions, such as stopping bleeding and alleviating diarrhea. Additionally, the root has been utilized as a food source during times of scarcity and as a natural dye to color leather red. The plant produces 2 to 8 dry, inedible fruits.
